newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE - Framatome seeks growth in nuclear services.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Framatome seeks growth in nuclear services.

text.p: The slowdown in the construction of nuclear power stations is forcing the French engineering group Framatome to expand nuclear services, concentrating on overseas markets.
Last month, Framatome hosted a New Nuclear Needs symposium, showing new products and techniques to clients ranging from the French power utility Electricite de France (EDF) to the Chinese state.

Framatome, the world's biggest constructor of nuclear power stations, is competing against such companies as Westinghouse and General Electric of the United States, the Swiss-Swedish ABB consortium and Germany's Siemens AG.

Teams of Framatome staff are wooing the Chinese for "another" nuclear project there -- following two orders to Framatome for Daya Bay and Ling Ao and one for Atomic Energy of Canada Ltd (AECL) for Qinshan. Such multi-billion dollar contracts are few and far between.
Nuclear services, however, generate a steady and regular stream of income. In 1995, the company made 2.9 billion francs ($560.7 million) in sales on Framatome's 17.9 billion francs sales total.
Dominique Vignon, managing director nuclear projects, said he expected the division's share of total sales would increase.
"With the ageing of the installed nuclear power plant base it would be logical to expect more demand for preventive maintenance services," he said.

Leading reporters around the exhibition of various control, maintenance and repair equipment for nuclear power stations at the CETIC site in Chalon-sur-Saone, Vignon stressed that none of the emergencies Framatome made contingencies for had ever happened.

There were machines that can treat a crack in the reactor vessel, remotely-controlled so that the operator will not be exposed to radiation. There were also tiny sensors that can gauge whether cracks are appearing and robots to execute complicated and dangerous alterations to the steam generators.
"What we sell is assurance," Vignon said.

"We try to imagine what kind of problems could occur with a nuclear station and then we develop equipment for it. That can take several years but we will have something ready if needed," said Daniele Hertzog, the head of the nuclear services units.
"We can't wait for an emergency call from a client and then try to cobble something together," she added.
The level of assurance depends on the client and culture. In France, Sweden, Belgium and Spain the level of precaution is quite high.

"The Americans just go on until it (a part) falls apart. At the other end of the scale, EDF is very much into preventive maintenance," Vignon said, explaing that the U.S. system of regulation on power utilities made it easier to obtain approval for replacement than for maintenance spending.

An example of EDF's culture of prevention is the CETIC site itself, a 50/50 joint-venture between the operator and Framatome. On the site are life-size models of nuclear equipment including an enormous pool representing a reactor cavity.
The models allow power station operators to train their employees in a non-radiated environment for tasks they have, or might have, to carry out in a "hostile" environment.

There are 434 nuclear power stations in the world of which more than half are of the pressurised water type. Of these, 203 are of the western PWR type and 40 of the Russian VVER concept in east and central Europe.

When building power stations abroad, Framatome usually works in tandem with such groups as EDF, the Anglo-French 50/50 industrial power joint venture GEC Alsthom of Alcatel Alsthom and Britain's GEC Plc.
But the company appreciates its freedom to be able to do deals from time to time with Siemens AG of Germany, a rival of GEC Alsthom.
Framatome officials are following the negotiations by the French state and GEC Alsthom to obtain control of their company with some apprehension.
Alcatel Alsthom has a 44 percent stake in Framatome.
The French government in late August approved a merger study between Framatome and GEC Alsthom.

Under a complex deal, Alcatel would become the largest shareholder in GEC Alsthom with some 47 percent, while GEC would have 37 percent. Other French Framatome stakeholders EDF, CEA Industrie and CDR would have 15 percent in the enlarged GEC Alsthom.

Alcatel Alsthom chairman Serge Tchuruk has said that he wants to float part of GEC Alsthom to give the company's management a clear focus and a level of independence they are not enjoying under the double parentage.
GEC Alsthom chairman Pierre Bilger said that Framatome's technology links with Siemens to develop a new European nuclear power station were important and would be continued.

Industry Minister Franck Borotra on November 6 fired Framatome chairman Jean-Claude Deny after he had openly criticised the planned merger. He will be replaced by Vignon on December 4. ($1=5.172 French Franc)
